title: The Determinant of a Linear Operator, Cofactors and Cramer's Rule

items.title: An alternating top-degree form is determined by its value on one ordered basis
items.strategy: Let B=(b_0,...,b_{n-1}) be an ordered basis of the positive-dimensional space V. For an alternating n-linear form omega, define F(A) by applying omega to the vectors whose B-coordinate columns are the columns of A. Then F is alternating and column-multilinear, so the published rigidity lemma gives F(A)=F(I_n)det(A). Substituting the coordinate matrix M_B(v_0,...,v_{n-1}) yields omega(v_0,...,v_{n-1})=omega(B)det(M_B(v_0,...,v_{n-1})). No exterior power is introduced.

items.title: The determinant of an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space, defined from its matrix in an ordered basis
On a positive-dimensional space, det(T) is the unique scalar by which T scales every alternating top-degree form
items.strategy: For an alternating n-linear form omega on a positive-dimensional n-dimensional space, put omega_T(v_0,...,v_{n-1})=omega(Tv_0,...,Tv_{n-1}). Apply the preceding coordinate formula first to omega_T and then to omega on the tuple (Tb_0,...,Tb_{n-1}); the coordinate matrix of that tuple is [T]_B, so omega_T=det([T]_B)omega=det(T)omega. For uniqueness, use the normalized coordinate form delta_B(v_0,...,v_{n-1})=det(M_B(v_0,...,v_{n-1})) and evaluate at B. Thus the theorem gives the honest top-form characterisation without defining exterior powers.

items.title: The determinant of a linear operator is independent of the chosen ordered basis
items.strategy: In positive dimension, the preceding theorem characterises the matrix-defined determinant as the unique scalar by which T scales every alternating top-degree form, a condition with no basis in its statement. Hence two ordered bases give the same scalar. Treat the zero-dimensional convention det(T)=1 separately.

items.title: For endomorphisms S and T of one finite-dimensional vector space, det(ST)=det(S)det(T)
items.strategy: For every alternating top-degree form omega, apply the scaling theorem first to S and then to T: omega(STv_0,...,STv_{n-1})=det(S)det(T)omega(v_0,...,v_{n-1}). Uniqueness in the same theorem identifies the scalar with det(ST). The zero-dimensional case reads 1=1 times 1.

items.title: The determinant of an operator can be computed from any representing matrix by row reduction while tracking swaps and row scalings
items.strategy: Choose any basis, row-reduce its representing matrix to echelon form, and use the published determinant effects of row operations and the diagonal product for a triangular matrix. Basis independence licenses the initial choice; row additions contribute no factor.

items.title: Deleted-row-and-column minors, cofactors, the cofactor matrix and the adjugate over a commutative ring
Laplace expansion computes the determinant along every row and every column over a commutative ring
items.strategy: For a fixed row, partition the Leibniz sum according to the selected column, delete that row and column, and identify the permutation sign with the cofactor sign. Obtain the column formula either by the same partition or by applying the row formula to the transpose and using determinant invariance under transpose. Include n=1 using the empty-minor convention.

items.title: For every positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring, A adj(A)=adj(A) A=det(A) I
items.strategy: Compute each entry of A adj(A). A diagonal entry is the Laplace expansion along the corresponding row; an off-diagonal entry is the same cofactor sum for a matrix with one row replaced by another, hence has determinant zero by alternation. Apply the column version for adj(A)A. Do not infer the off-diagonal zeros merely from singularity over a ring.

items.title: A positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring is invertible if and only if its determinant is a unit
items.strategy: The forward implication is the published unit-determinant corollary. Conversely, if u=det(A) is a unit, multiply the adjugate identity by u^{-1} to exhibit u^{-1}adj(A) as a two-sided inverse.

items.title: If det(A) is a unit, then A^{-1}=det(A)^{-1} adj(A)
items.strategy: Scale both sides of the two adjugate identities by the inverse of det(A), and invoke uniqueness of a two-sided matrix inverse.

items.title: For A in M_n(R) and columns u,v over a commutative ring, det(A+uv^T)=det(A)+v^T adj(A)u
items.strategy: Expand det(A+uv^T) multilinearly in its columns. The empty choice gives det(A); every term choosing two or more columns from uv^T vanishes because those columns are scalar multiples of u. For the singleton choice j, expand the determinant with column j replaced by u along that column, obtaining v_j sum_i C_ij u_i. Summing over j is v^T adj(A)u. State n>=1 explicitly.

items.title: Over a commutative ring, adj(P^{-1}AP)=P^{-1}adj(A)P for every invertible P
items.strategy: Put C=P^{-1}AP. Compare det(C+uv^T) in two ways. The rank-one update formula gives det(C)+v^T adj(C)u. Similarity invariance rewrites it as det(A+(Pu)(v^T P^{-1})), and a second rank-one update gives det(A)+v^T P^{-1}adj(A)Pu. Cancel det(C)=det(A), then choose u and v to be standard coordinate columns to identify every entry. This works for singular A and avoids any undeveloped rational-function field.

items.title: For A in M_n(R), the coordinate endomorphism T_A:R^n to R^n, with det(T_A):=det(A) and adj(T_A):=T_adj(A)
Cramer's rule over a commutative ring: every solution satisfies det(A)x_j=det(A_j(b)), and a unit determinant gives the unique quotient formula
items.strategy: For Ax=b, replace column j of A by b and use b=sum_k x_k A_k. Column multilinearity kills every term except k=j, giving det(A_j(b))=x_j det(A). If det(A) is a unit, the adjugate formula constructs the solution with those coordinates and invertibility gives uniqueness. State n>=1 and do not divide by a merely nonzero non-unit.

items.title: Over a field, for each right-hand side b, Ax=b has a unique solution exactly when det(A) is nonzero, and then Cramer's quotient formula holds
items.strategy: If det(A) is nonzero, it is a unit and the ring theorem supplies the unique Cramer solution. Conversely, if Ax=b has one unique solution x, every z in the kernel would make x+z another solution, so the kernel is zero; the invertible-matrix theorem makes A invertible, and the determinant is nonzero. State n>=1.

items.title: A finite-dimensional linear operator over a field is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero
items.strategy: Choose a basis. The operator is invertible exactly when its representing matrix is invertible; over a field the unit-determinant criterion is the nonzero-determinant criterion. The unique endomorphism of the zero space is invertible and has determinant 1.

items.title: Determinant is a group homomorphism GL(V) to F^times, and det(T^{-1})=det(T)^{-1}
items.strategy: Multiplicativity and det(I)=1 put invertible operators in the unit group. Apply multiplicativity to TT^{-1}=I to obtain the inverse formula.

items.title: The adjugate of an operator on a positive-dimensional finite-dimensional vector space, defined by the adjugate matrix in any basis
For a positive-dimensional finite-dimensional operator, T adj(T)=adj(T)T=det(T) I
items.strategy: Choose a basis and take matrices. The two composites have matrices A adj(A) and adj(A)A, which equal det(A)I by the ring-level adjugate identity; basis independence identifies det(A) with det(T). Equality of representing matrices gives equality of operators.

title: The Determinant of a Linear Operator, Cofactors and Cramer's Rule: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A nonidentity projection of the plane has determinant zero and is not invertible
items.strategy: For T(x,y)=(x,0), compute the diagonal matrix diag(1,0), its determinant, kernel and image, and compare with the operator invertibility criterion.

items.title: One operator has matrices diag(2,3) and [[2,0],[1,3]] in two bases, both with determinant 6
items.strategy: Take T(x,y)=(2x,3y), the standard basis E, and B=((1,1),(0,1)). Compute P_{E<-B}, P^{-1}AP, and both determinants explicitly, checking the abstract change-of-basis proof numerically.

items.title: Multiplication by 2 on Z is injective but not surjective: its determinant is the non-unit 2, its adjugate is integral, and its inverse exists only over Q
items.strategy: Represent n->2n by the 1 by 1 integer matrix [2]. Its determinant is 2 and its adjugate is [1]. Cancellation in Z proves injectivity, while 1 has no preimage proves nonsurjectivity; over Q the inverse matrix is [1/2].

items.title: FALSE: a square matrix over a commutative ring is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero
items.strategy: Refute the reverse implication with the preceding integer example: the one-by-one matrix [2] has nonzero determinant 2 in Z, but 2 is not a unit and multiplication by 2 is not surjective. The forward implication also needs a nonzero-ring hypothesis, since over the zero ring the one-by-one identity matrix is [0], is invertible, and has determinant 0. Contrast both failures with the proved unit criterion, which is the correct statement for every commutative ring.

items.title: A sparse 4 by 4 determinant is 30 by both cofactor expansion and row reduction
items.strategy: Use A=[[1,2,0,0],[0,3,0,0],[4,8,2,1],[0,0,0,5]]. Expand along the last row and then a sparse column to obtain 30. Separately replace row 3 by row 3 minus 4 row 1, producing a triangular matrix with diagonal 1,3,2,5 and no determinant-changing operation.

items.title: The adjugate gives the inverse of a three by three rational matrix with determinant 3
items.strategy: For A=[[1,2,0],[0,1,1],[1,0,1]], compute the cofactor matrix [[1,1,-1],[-2,1,2],[2,-1,1]], transpose it to adj(A)=[[1,-2,2],[1,1,-1],[-1,2,1]], and verify A adj(A)=3I. Since 3 is a unit in Q, conclude A^{-1}=(1/3)adj(A) and multiply once more to check.

items.title: Cramer's rule solves 2x+y=5 and x-y=1 as (x,y)=(2,1)
items.strategy: For A=[[2,1],[1,-1]] and b=(5,1), compute det(A)=-3, the two replacement determinants -6 and -3, divide in Q or R, and verify the resulting pair in both equations.

items.title: Determinant is additive in one selected column but not under simultaneous whole-matrix addition
items.strategy: Over Z, take u=(1,0)^T, v=(0,1)^T and w=(0,1)^T. The two-by-two formula gives det([u+v,w])=1=det([u,w])+det([v,w])=1+0, illustrating valid additivity in the first column while the second is fixed. Then directly compute with A=B=I_2 that det(A+B)=4 but det(A)+det(B)=2. The paired computations isolate exactly why columnwise multilinearity is not linearity in the whole matrix argument.

title: The Integral Logarithm and the Equivalence of Its Characterisations

items.title: The integral logarithm L(x):=integral from 1 to x of dt/t for x>0
The integral logarithm satisfies L'(x)=1/x for x>0 and L(1)=0
items.strategy: Choose a compact positive interval containing both x and 1. Additivity and the orientation convention rewrite L near x as a constant plus an integral function with a fixed lower endpoint, so the first FTC gives L'(x)=1/x on either side of 1. The oriented integral from 1 to 1 is zero. No exponential or logarithm result is cited.

items.title: The integral logarithm is continuous and strictly increasing on (0,infinity)
items.strategy: Differentiability gives continuity. For 0<a<b, the mean value theorem gives L(b)-L(a)=(b-a)/c for some c in (a,b), which is positive.

items.title: The integral logarithm satisfies L(xy)=L(x)+L(y) for all positive x and y
items.strategy: Fix y>0 and set h(x)=L(xy)-L(x). By the chain rule and L'=1/x, h'(x)=y/(xy)-1/x=0. The zero-derivative theorem makes h constant, and h(1)=L(y)-L(1)=L(y). This proof deliberately uses no substitution theorem and no exponential.

items.title: L(1/x)=-L(x), L(x^n)=nL(x), and in particular L(2^n)=nL(2)
items.strategy: Apply the product law to x(1/x)=1 for reciprocals and induct on the natural exponent for powers, with n=0 using L(1)=0. Negative integer powers follow from reciprocals. Since L is strictly increasing, L(2)>0.

items.title: The integral logarithm is unbounded above and below
items.strategy: Because L(2)>0, the Archimedean property makes nL(2) exceed any prescribed real bound. The power formula identifies this value with L(2^n), and the reciprocal formula gives L(2^{-n})=-nL(2) for the lower bound. No exponential is used.

items.title: L:(0,infinity) to R is a continuous strictly increasing bijection
items.strategy: Strict increase gives injectivity. For a target r, choose positive a<b with L(a)<r<L(b) using two-sided unboundedness, then apply the intermediate value theorem on [a,b] for surjectivity. Continuity comes from differentiability.

items.title: The integral exponential E:R to (0,infinity) as the inverse of L
The inverse E satisfies E(a+b)=E(a)E(b)
items.strategy: The product law gives L(E(a)E(b))=a+b=L(E(a+b)); injectivity of L gives the result. This remains entirely inside the integral construction.

items.title: The inverse E is differentiable, E'=E, and E(0)=1
items.strategy: Apply the derivative-of-an-inverse theorem to L at E(y): E'(y)=1/L'(E(y))=E(y). Since L(1)=0 and E is its inverse, E(0)=1. This proof contains no reference to the published exponential.

items.title: The integral exponential E is the published exponential function
items.strategy: The preceding theorem gives E'=E and E(0)=1. Invoke thm-exponential-ivp-uniqueness once to conclude E=exp. This is the sole bridge from the integral construction to exp.

items.title: The integral logarithm L is the published natural logarithm
items.strategy: L is the inverse of E, E=exp by the bridge theorem, and the published log is defined as exp^{-1}; uniqueness of inverse functions gives L=log.

items.title: The number e is the unique x>0 satisfying integral from 1 to x of dt/t=1
items.strategy: Since E=exp, E(1)=exp(1)=e. Inverse identities give L(e)=1, and strict increase of L gives uniqueness.

items.title: Log is the unique continuous f:(0,infinity) to R with f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) and f(e)=1
items.strategy: Set g(t)=f(E(t)). The integral-exponential addition law makes g additive, and E is continuous because E is differentiable. Cauchy regularity gives g(t)=ct. The single bridge gives E(1)=exp(1)=e, so g(1)=f(e)=1 fixes c=1. For x>0, x=E(L(x)), hence f(x)=L(x)=log x. Conversely, the published log has the required law, continuity and normalisation.

items.title: Log is the unique f with f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) that is differentiable at 1 with f'(1)=1
items.strategy: The functional equation gives f(1)=0. Rewriting f(x+h)-f(x)=f(1+h/x)-f(1) and scaling the difference quotient proves differentiability at every x with f'(x)=f'(1)/x=1/x. Therefore (f-L)'=0 and f(1)=L(1)=0, so f=L=log.

items.title: Every continuous f with f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) is f(x)=c log x for a unique c, including c=0
items.strategy: Apply the same transport g=f composed with E. The addition law and continuity of E make g continuous and additive, so Cauchy regularity gives g(t)=ct with c=g(1)=f(e). For x>0, x=E(L(x)) gives f(x)=cL(x)=c log x. Uniqueness follows by evaluating at e. For c nonzero this is the constant-multiple form underlying logarithms to other bases; c=0 is the trivial solution and requires no division.

items.title: The Mercator series, its value at 1 and the product law determine log on all positive reals, while the series alone is only local
items.strategy: For every x>0, use the Archimedean property to choose a natural k with 0<x/2^k<2, then write x=2^k(1+u) with |u|<1. Any product-law function agreeing with the Mercator series on 1+u and at 2 must have f(x)=k f(2)+f(1+u), so at most one extension exists; the published log series and log laws supply existence. State explicitly that this is continuation data, not convergence of the original series at x-1.

items.title: Five characterisations of the natural logarithm are equivalent: inverse exponential, integral, continued Mercator series, Landau root limit and the normalised functional equation
items.strategy: Use the single E=exp bridge and inversion for the integral characterisation; cite the published Mercator and Landau theorems for their local or pointwise formulas; use the extension lemma to state exactly what extra product-law data makes the series global; and use the continuous functional-equation uniqueness theorem for the fifth characterisation. Distinguish full-domain definitions from the local series plus continuation rule.

items.title: Roadmap and non-circularity of the logarithm characterisations

title: The Integral Logarithm and Its Characterisations: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Log 2 from four characterisations: hyperbolic area, the alternating harmonic series, Landau iterates and exp^{-1}(2)
items.strategy: List the four equal quantities integral_1^2 dt/t, sum_{n>=1}(-1)^{n+1}/n, lim 2^n(2^{1/2^n}-1), and the unique y with exp(y)=2. Cite the A-page series and Landau results directly, not the already-published B-page example, and identify all four through the equivalence theorem.

items.title: Dropping f(e)=1 leaves the whole family c log, including logarithms to other bases and the zero function
items.strategy: Verify directly that c log(xy)=c log x+c log y, compute f(e)=c, and compare c=1/log b with log_b for b>0, b not equal to 1. Include c=0 to show why the family is slightly larger than base logarithms.

items.title: Assuming choice, a Hamel-basis additive map transported through exp gives a discontinuous logarithmic function that is not c log
items.strategy: From a Hamel basis choose a coefficient map g:R->R that is additive and not scalar multiplication. Define f(exp t)=g(t), which is well-defined because exp is bijective. The exponential law gives f(xy)=f(x)+f(y). If f were continuous, then g=f composed with exp would be continuous and Cauchy regularity would force g to be scalar, a contradiction.

items.title: For every x>2 the uncontinued Mercator series at u=x-1 diverges
items.strategy: For u=x-1>1, the absolute ratio of successive terms u^n/n tends to u>1; the ratio test gives divergence (equivalently the terms do not tend to zero). Contrast this with the product-law continuation in the A-page lemma.

items.title: Integral bounds alone give 2<e<4; the sharper published bound is 2<e<3
items.strategy: Split [1,2] at 3/2. Monotonicity gives 7/12<=L(2)<=5/6, hence L(2)<1 and L(4)=2L(2)>1. Since L(e)=1 and L is strictly increasing, 2<e<4. Cite, but do not reprove, the sharper 2<e<3 corollary.
